implementation_notes: Mark the model class @Observable: any property a view body reads becomes a tracked dependency and the view re-renders when it changes, including computed properties that read observable properties. No change notifications are written by hand; commands are plain methods, and the view holds the model with @State or takes it from the environment. The model imports only Observation, so tests exercise it directly. This is the current form for deployment targets of iOS 17 / macOS 14 and later.
pitfalls: Observation tracks only properties read during body: state read in an escaping closure or a callback creates no dependency, so changes there are not rendered (the SwiftUI documentation is explicit that the view tracks what body reads).
A view that only passes the observable object through without reading a property does not update when its properties change - the documented pass-through case.
UI-bound state must be mutated on the main actor; mark the model @MainActor or hop back before writing observed properties from background work.

variants.name: ObservableObject with @Published and SwiftUI property wrappers
variants.implementation_notes: Before Observation, the model conformed to ObservableObject and marked its fields @Published; SwiftUI subscribed through the generated objectWillChange publisher (Combine) and re-rendered, with @StateObject (ownership) or @ObservedObject (handed in) controlling lifetime. Choose it when deployment targets predate iOS 17 / macOS 14; the model still holds no view types, but the conformance and the property wrappers must be written and kept correct, and a missed @Published silently stops updates.
pitfalls: A stored property changed without @Published does not publish, so the view silently stops updating for that field.
Manual objectWillChange subscriptions hold the model strongly unless the subscription is stored as AnyCancellable and cancelled on teardown.
Creating the model inside body with @ObservedObject recreates it on every render and discards its state; @StateObject exists to own it exactly once.
